title: Fish, Herring and Golce
lead: Pomeranian cuisine is the taste of the Baltic meeting Hanseatic tradition. Find out what is worth eating on the coast — from herring to golce. Slow travel through Pomeranian cuisine.
body:
Why Pomeranian cuisine, differently

Pomeranian cuisine is the cuisine of a coastal region — based on Baltic fish, potatoes, and cabbage, with influences from Kashubian, Kociewie, and Żuławy cuisines. It is simple, hearty, but at the same time diverse — from fish specialties to thick soups. Pomerania is a region of northern Poland, around Gdańsk and Gdynia, where for centuries Kashubians, Kociewians, Żuławians, and Germans lived side by side — and each of these cultures brought something to the local cuisine.

Slow travel through Pomeranian cuisine is a celebration of taste and tradition. Instead of rushing from restaurant to restaurant, stop in one longer — in a fish shop by the harbour, in a village inn, in an agritourism farm. Each dish has its own story, its own cook, its own fishing village. Ask where the fish comes from, how the dish is prepared, who passed down the recipe. This is a journey that rewards those who slow down — the longer you are in one place, the more flavors you can truly get to know.

What to see

Pomeranian cuisine splits into several categories: Baltic fish (herring, cod, flounder), smoked fish (salmon, mackerel, eel), potato dishes (golce, pancakes), cabbage dishes (cabbage with mushrooms), soups (fish soup, żur), baked goods (Żuławy bread, szneki z glancem). Exploring the culinary region of Pomerania takes 2–3 days.

Baltic fish

  • Herring in oil — a classic of Pomeranian cuisine. Marinated herring, served with onion, oil, and potatoes in their jackets. There are many variations — in sour cream, in vinegar, with mustard. The best in small fish shops and fish bars by the sea.
  • Fresh cod — Baltic cod, fried or baked, with garlic sauce or butter. Worth it in small fish shops in Gdynia, Hel, Władysławowo.
  • Fried flounder — a flat Baltic fish, fried in a pan, served with fries, salad, and lemon. A classic of seaside fish shops.
  • Herring in sour cream — marinated herring served in thick sour cream with onion and apple. A classic of German cuisine, also adopted in Pomerania.

Smoked fish and potato dishes

  • Smoked salmon — salmon from the Baltic or from farms, traditionally smoked in home smokehouses. Served with bread, butter, and lemon.
  • Smoked mackerel — a cheap, tasty fish, smoked in home smokehouses. Available at smokehouses by the sea.
  • Smoked eel — expensive but with an exceptional flavor. If you see a smokehouse with eels by the road, it is usually worth stopping.
  • Golce — the Kashubian version of Silesian dumplings, potato balls with flour, boiled in water. Served with onion, lard, or mushroom sauce. Simple, filling, rural.
  • Potato pancakes — in the Pomeranian version with marjoram and bacon. Served with sour cream or mushroom sauce.

Soups, cabbage and baked goods

  • Fish soup — soup based on Baltic fish broth, with vegetables, potatoes, and sour cream. Served with croutons or bread.
  • Pomeranian żur — sour rye soup with white sausage and egg. A Pomeranian classic.
  • Cabbage with mushrooms — braised cabbage with dried mushrooms, onion, and caraway. Served with meats, especially game and roasts.
  • Żuławy bread — dark sourdough bread with rye and wheat flour. Characteristic of Żuławy — a depression region east of Gdańsk.
  • Szneki z glancem — sweet yeast buns with streusel and icing. Popular for breakfast throughout the region.

When to go

  • April–June — the best time for slow travel. Fewer tourists, fresh seasonal fish, long days. Worth a walk around fish shops.
  • July–September — season for fresh fish, fruit, mushrooms. Worth it for fish markets in Gdynia and Hel.
  • September–October — second best. Herring, smoked eel, fewer people. September is a good time for mushroom picking in Pomeranian forests.
  • November–March — season for herring, bigos, żur. Worth it for winter cuisine, especially during the holiday season.

Getting there

Pomeranian cuisine is from the northern region of Poland — best to travel by car or train, connecting several towns in one trip.

  • By train: Gdańsk, Gdynia, Sopot, Słupsk have railway stations, with connections from most Polish cities.
  • By car: ~4 hours from Warsaw (S7), ~3.5 hours from Poznań (S5 and A1), ~5 hours from Wrocław (S8 and S5).
  • By bus: PKS and private operators serve most towns on the route.

How much time you need

A weekend (2 days) is the minimum — Gdańsk or Gdynia (fish shops, herring, cod) and surroundings.

Three days is realistic for a first visit. Gdańsk, Gdynia, Sopot, Hel.

A week lets you explore the whole culinary region of Pomerania — all the most important dishes and places, and neighbouring Kashubia.

What to eat and where to sleep

Instead of restaurants, choose fish shops and village inns. There, cooks prepare what they have known since childhood, and they do it best.

  • Herring in oil — a Pomeranian classic, available at every fish shop.
  • Golce — the Kashubian version of dumplings, available at village inns.
  • Smoked eel — a regional delicacy, available at smokehouses by the sea.
  • Fish soup — a Pomeranian classic, available at every fish shop.
  • Żuławy bread — dark sourdough bread, available at bakeries in Gdańsk.
  • Beer from local breweries — several craft breweries in the region (Browar PG4, Browar Puck).

Accommodation: Gdańsk (largest choice, more options), Sopot (resort, more options), Gdynia (town, more options), Słupsk (town, more options), agritourism farms in villages (quiet, home-cooked food).

Practical tips

  • Fish shops — usually open from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., longer in season. Check hours before your trip.
  • Regional restaurants — look for places where cooks prepare traditional recipes. Avoid tourist restaurants in city centres.
  • Culinary workshops — many farms and agritourism businesses offer workshops (smoking fish, baking bread, making golce). Book ahead.
  • Diet — Pomeranian cuisine can be heavy and filling. Eat smaller portions to try more dishes.
  • Fish markets — the best place to buy fresh fish. Held regularly in Gdynia and Hel.
  • Weather — coastal weather changes fast. Even in July, bring a windproof jacket and hat.
  • Signal — good in towns, weaker in villages. Have an offline map.
tip: Order golce at one of the Pomeranian village inns — preferably the version with onion and lard, as it has been served in Pomerania for generations.
